common_name: Black Dragon Wisteria (Double Dark Purple Japanese Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a very sturdy, permanent arbor or pergola able to bear the mature vine's substantial weight.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun on an oversized permanent structure, since this vigorous Japanese wisteria becomes extremely heavy with age. Black Dragon is prized for fully double, deep violet-purple, intensely fragrant flowers carried on racemes to 18 inches, giving a fuller, ruffled look than single-flowered wisteria selections and a long, heavy floral display each spring. Like other Japanese wisterias it twines clockwise and grows with tremendous vigor, so plan for annual summer pruning after bloom to keep growth in bounds and a second dormant-season pruning to encourage the short spur growth that produces the best flowering. Give it years to reach flowering maturity, and keep an eye on root suckers and self-seeding, since Asian wisteria species can become weedy outside cultivation in warm, humid regions.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in rich, well-drained, non-alkaline soil in full sun to light shade on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Honbeni is slower-growing than most wisteria, making it a better fit for smaller structures.

directions: Plant in rich, non-alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun or part shade on a sturdy support; unlike most wisteria, Honbeni (sold under the trade name Pink Ice) is a comparatively restrained grower, typically adding only 2-3 feet of new growth per year, which makes it a realistic choice for a modest arbor or fence rather than a massive pergola. The pale pink, lavender-edged flowers with a soft yellow center hang in long racemes up to 16 inches and carry the classic sweet wisteria fragrance, opening as the bronze-tinted new foliage matures to green. Prune lightly right after the spring bloom to shape the vine and remove any wayward shoots, and provide a permanent structure from the start since even a slow-growing wisteria becomes heavy and long-lived over decades.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moderately fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to part shade on a very sturdy, permanent arbor or pergola.

directions: Grow in moderately fertile, well-drained, medium-moisture soil in full sun or part shade on an oversized, permanent structure able to carry substantial long-term weight. Caroline is valued for blooming earlier in spring than most wisteria selections and for reliably flowering at a younger age, producing deep purple, sweetly fragrant racemes 6-12 inches long that attract bees and butterflies in large numbers. Nursery sources list its parentage variously as Japanese, Chinese, or hybrid wisteria, so treat it with the same caution as other Asian-derived wisterias regarding vigorous growth and potential to seed or sucker outside cultivation. Prune twice a year, once immediately after bloom and again in late winter, to control its vigorous twining growth and to encourage the short spurs that carry next year's flowers.

common_name: Blanche Sandman Trumpet Honeysuckle (Orange-Red Coral Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or mailbox post; twining stems climb 10-20 feet and benefit from initial tying-in until established.

directions: Plant in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun for best bloom, though it tolerates light shade. Selected at Holbrook Farm Nursery in North Carolina, Blanche Sandman bears an especially heavy display of rich orange-red tubular flowers with bright yellow throats in spring, with light rebloom through summer, followed by small red berries that songbirds enjoy. The blue-green, semi-evergreen foliage and long, twining stems make it excellent for quickly covering a fence, mailbox post, or pergola, and unlike Japanese honeysuckle, this native selection is well-behaved and does not spread invasively. Prune right after the main spring flush to control size and shape, and deadhead lightly to encourage continued summer flowering.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun against a large, permanent arbor, wall, or fence; like the species, Judy climbs by aerial rootlets and spreads by root suckers, so site it away from structures you don't want it to grip.

directions: Grow in rich, well-drained soil in full sun against a strong permanent support, since this vigorous woody vine self-clings tightly with aerial rootlets and becomes very heavy over time. Introduced by Woodlanders Nursery, Judy is a Southeastern native selection prized for large, yellow-apricot trumpet flowers with reddish-orange throats that appear from summer into fall, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies in steady numbers. It is just as vigorous and heat-tolerant as the wild orange-red species, spreading by root suckers and self-clinging to masonry, siding, and tree bark, so give it a dedicated structure well away from the house. Cut back hard in late winter each year to control size and encourage a strong flush of new flowering wood.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade against a trellis, arbor, or fence, since Akebia twines and does not self-cling.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade with a trellis or arbor for the twining stems to climb, since this vine does not cling on its own. Alba is the white-flowered form of chocolate vine, producing dangling clusters of pure white, vanilla-and-chocolate-scented flowers in mid-spring against dark green, five-parted leaves, followed in fall by unusual sausage-shaped purple seed pods when cross-pollinated with another Akebia. It is semi-evergreen in mild climates and fully deciduous farther north, growing vigorously enough to need an annual pruning after bloom to keep it within bounds and off nearby shrubs or trees. Because Akebia self-pollinates poorly, planting a second cultivar nearby, such as the species or a differently colored selection, greatly improves fruit set if pods are desired.

common_name: Amethyst Glow Chocolate Vine (Purple-Flowered Five-Leaf Akebia)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade against a trellis or arbor for the twining stems to climb.

directions: Grow in any good, well-drained garden soil in sun or part shade, training the twining stems onto a trellis, arbor, or fence. Amethyst Glow bears fragrant, rich purple female flowers alongside smaller, paler pink male flowers on the same raceme in early spring, a two-toned effect that sets it apart from single-color Akebia selections, and the rounded, blue-green-backed leaflets take on a purple tint in winter. Given a long, hot summer and a nearby cross-pollinator, it can set purple, sausage-shaped edible-pulp fruit in fall, though most gardeners grow it for the flowers and fast-covering foliage alone. This is a vigorous semi-evergreen climber, so prune after flowering each year to keep it off nearby structures and shrubs.

common_name: Silver Bells Chocolate Vine (White-and-Purple Five-Leaf Akebia)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to mostly shady sites against a trellis or arbor; Silver Bells tolerates more shade than many flowering vines.

directions: Plant in average, rich, well-drained soil in anything from full sun to mostly shade, providing a trellis or arbor since the twining stems do not cling on their own. Silver Bells produces creamy white, bell-shaped flowers with deep purple interiors and a sweet vanilla-chocolate fragrance in early spring, opening as the purple-tinged new leaflets emerge and mature to blue-green. It is a vigorous semi-evergreen grower capable of reaching 15 feet or more in a season once established, and can produce purplish-blue, sausage-shaped fruit with edible white pulp when cross-pollinated with another Akebia selection. Prune back hard after flowering each year to control its spread and keep it from smothering nearby plants or structures.

common_name: Adam Kiwi Vine (Male Pollinator Variegated Kolomikta Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant one male Adam vine for every 6-8 female kolomikta kiwi vines in spring in rich, well-drained, non-alkaline soil, siting it in a sheltered spot such as an east- or southeast-facing wall to protect the ornamental foliage.

directions: Grow in rich, moist, well-drained, non-calcareous soil with a sturdy trellis or wall support, siting it out of harsh afternoon sun since kolomikta foliage can scorch in full exposure. Adam is a Polish-bred male selection grown strictly as a pollinator for female Arctic Beauty kiwi cultivars such as Eve, and it does not itself produce fruit, but it more than earns its space with striking foliage variegated in shades of pink, cream-white, and green that rivals or exceeds most female selections for ornamental impact. Small, lightly citrus-scented white flowers with yellow stamens open in late spring and are visited readily by bees carrying pollen to nearby female vines. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than typical kolomikta seedlings, so provide winter wind protection in the coldest parts of its range and prune lightly after flowering to maintain a manageable, well-branched framework.
